food.text: Pellegrino Artusi's La scienza in cucina e l'arte di mangiare bene, first published in 1891, is widely regarded as the canon of classic modern Italian cuisine. Its recipes come mostly from Romagna and Tuscany, where he lived. The book is still in print.

Italian cuisine can trace its roots to the 4th century BC, but the country known as Italy did not unite until the 19th century. Around 1880, two decades after unification, the Italian diaspora began. With it, Italian cuisine started to spread around the world.
Gian Battista and Giovanni Ratto's La cucina genovese, published in 1871, addressed the cuisine of Liguria. This book contained the first recipe for pesto.

In the 19th century, Giovanni Vialardi, chef to King Victor Emmanuel II, wrote a treatise on modern cookery with recipes "suitable for a modest household". Many of his recipes were regional dishes from Turin, including 12 for potatoes.
Ippolito Cavalcanti wrote La cucina teorico-pratica, The Theoretical-Practical Cuisine. It described the first recipe for pasta with tomatoes, a pairing now familiar around the world.

Some believe supplì, the Roman snack of a rice ball with tomato sauce, derive from French croquettes. They think the French troops of Napoleon introduced them to Rome at the beginning of the 19th century.

In 1829, Giovanni Felice Luraschi's Il nuovo cuoco milanese economico (The New Economic Milanese Chef) featured Milanese dishes. Among them were kidney with anchovies and lemon, and gnocchi alla romana.

Pinzimonio is an Italian dip of olive oil, salt and pepper served with raw vegetables. During the Renaissance, produce decorating banquets came to be dipped in the sauces of the dishes it adorned. By the 19th century the dip was replaced with olive oil.

The name supplì is first attested in the 19th century. It is an Italianization of the French word surprise, a corruption of en surprise, a term used in French cuisine for croquettes and breadcrumb-covered pieces of meat.

art.text: The Macchiaioli were painters from Tuscany who broke with the antiquated conventions of the Italian art academies. They painted outdoors to capture natural light, shade and colour. They were forerunners of the Impressionists, who began pursuing similar aims in France in the 1860s.

In the 19th century Italy went through socio-economic change, several foreign invasions and the turbulent Risorgimento, which ended in Italian unification in 1861. Italian art shifted through many styles along the way, marking the transition from Enlightenment to Romanticism.

Milan's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, built in 1865, was the first building in iron, glass and steel in Italy. It is also the world's oldest purpose-built shopping gallery. It later influenced the Galleria Umberto I in Naples.

The stile Umbertino was named after King Umberto I, who reigned over the Kingdom of Italy from 1878 until 1900. It covered architecture, furniture and other decorative arts, and it was most popular in Rome. It was the Italian version of Eclecticism, which mixed features from different historical styles.

The Macchiaioli, a 19th-century Italian art movement, influenced French impressionism. They believed that areas of light and shadow, called "macchie", meaning patches or spots, were the chief components of a work of art.

Milan became a major European artistic centre in the Romantic period, influenced by the Austrians who ruled it at the time. Probably the most notable Romantic work held there is "The Kiss" by Francesco Hayez, kept in the Brera Academy.

After Italian unification, the stile Umbertino aspired to be distinctively Italian, as one of many attempts to build a national sense of unity. It was often used for ministries, law courts, palaces and villas. Rome became the new capital in 1870, and the city council and government planned a grand redevelopment of the city.

The Macchiaioli believed that areas of light and shadow, called "macchie" (patches or spots), were the chief components of a work of art. Their most notable artists were Giovanni Fattori, Silvestro Lega and Telemaco Signorini.

Italian Neoclassical buildings from these decades include the San Carlo Theatre in Naples (1810), the Pedrocchi Café in Padua (1816) and the Teatro Carlo Felice in Genoa (1827). Another is the Cisternone in Livorno (1829). Luigi Cagnola's Arco della Pace in Milan is also listed among them.

Antonio Canova, the main figure of European neoclassicism, was educated partly at the Venice Academy and in Rome. Italy's influence on sculpture drew Americans there because of its monuments, ruins and collections. Working conditions were far better than in the New World, which lacked marble and skilled stone-carving assistants.

Napoleon Bonaparte, who ruled most of Italy in the early 19th century, hired the neoclassical sculptor Antonio Canova to make sculptures for him. One of the most famous was Venus Victrix, an allegory of Pauline Bonaparte.

The Umbertino style was a particularly conservative kind of Eclecticism, aiming at a truly national style. It came to be identified with an academic Renaissance Revival repertoire, with elements drawn from the Baroque and early Renaissance. It gained popularity after 1870 and dwindled around 1895.

Horatio Greenough was the first of a large wave of American sculptors to settle between Rome and Florence. After 1857 William Wetmore Story led the American colony in Rome and became a reference point for every newcomer. Their work kept receiving press coverage at home until the neoclassical vogue faded in North America from the 1870s.

The early Macchiaioli were ridiculed, and many of the artists died in penury, only achieving fame towards the end of the 19th century. Today their work is much better known in Italy than elsewhere, and much of it sits in private collections there.

The manifesto Del purismo nelle arti, dated 1842–43, was written by Antonio Bianchini. It was co-signed by Tommaso Minardi, the major proponent of Purismo, together with Nazarene co-founder Friedrich Overbeck and Pietro Tenerani.

war.text: In 1866, Italy declared war on Austria in alliance with Prussia. When the war was won, Italy received the region of Veneto.

Italian troops entered Rome in 1870, ending more than one thousand years of Papal temporal power. The Kingdom of Italy took the city only after several battles and guerrilla-like warfare, as Papal Zouaves and the official troops of the Holy See fought the Italian invaders. France had abandoned its positions protecting Rome and Pius IX to fight the Prussians in the Franco-Prussian War.

Italy fought three wars of independence against the Austrian Empire, in 1848 to 1849, 1859 and 1866. Even after these, Trento and Trieste remained under Austrian rule. They became the main "irredent lands" of a movement that demanded their annexation.

In 1882, Italy entered a Triple Alliance with the German Empire and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, after strong disagreements with France over colonial expansion. The alliance with Vienna stayed purely formal, partly because Italy wanted to acquire Trentino and Trieste from Austria-Hungary.

In the Second Italian War of Independence of 1859, the Kingdom of Sardinia attacked the Austrian Empire with the aid of France. The war liberated Lombardy. Under the Plombières Agreement, Sardinia ceded Savoy and Nice to France.

Italy sent troops to China as part of the Eight-Nation Alliance during the Boxer Rebellion, from 2 November 1899 to 7 September 1901. On 7 September 1901 the Qing Dynasty ceded a concession in Tientsin to Italy. Italy took it into possession on 7 June 1902, and an Italian consul administered it.

The Fasci Siciliani was a popular democratic and socialist movement that arose in Sicily in 1892 and 1893. It was crushed after harsh military operations in 1894. Prime Minister Francesco Crispi also pushed through exceptional laws against the Socialists from 1894.
The 1859 deal over Nice caused the Niçard exodus, in which a quarter of the Niçard Italians emigrated to Italy. It was one of the human consequences of the Plombières Agreement.

In 1871, Giuseppe Garibaldi was elected in Nice to the National Assembly, but he was prevented from speaking when he tried to promote annexing his hometown to Italy. Riots followed in 1871 and 1872, called the "Niçard Vespers". Fifteen people who took part in the rebellion were tried and sentenced.
In 1912, the Partito Socialista Riformista Italiano split off from the Italian Socialist Party. For patriotic reasons, it agreed to the war against the Ottomans.

literature.text: Sibilla Aleramo published her first novel, Una Donna (A Woman), in 1906. Today it is widely acknowledged as Italy's premier feminist novel. Her writing mixes together autobiographical and fictional elements.

Italian writers of the 19th century, including Leopardi and Alessandro Manzoni, detested being grouped into a category of writing. As a result, Italy was home to many isolated literary figures. The term Romanticism itself had no unambiguous meaning there.

Anna Maria Mozzoni triggered a widespread women's movement in Italy by publishing Woman and her social relationships in 1864, on the occasion of the revision of the Italian Civil Code. Her book raised awareness of injustices in Italian family law that discriminated against women.
tags: La donna e i suoi rapporti sociali

literature.text: The Italian romantic school had as its organ the Conciliatore, established in 1818 at Milan. Its staff included Silvio Pellico, Ludovico di Breme, Giovanni Berchet and Alessandro Manzoni. All were influenced by ideas that, especially in Germany, made up the movement called Romanticism.

Beginning in 1868 at the age of 26, Alaide Gualberta Beccari began publishing the journal Women in Venice. She spent much of the 1870s and 1880s spreading information about feminism, and male legislators and teachers were among her growing readership.

Beccari's journal covered international feminist news, such as the political and social gains being made by women in France, the United States, and Great Britain. In 1877, a series of her articles on pro-reform topics inspired 3000 women to sign a petition for women's suffrage.

Anna Maria Mozzoni also translated John Stuart Mill's On the Subjugation of Women into Italian. She campaigned against state regulation of prostitution, and in 1881 founded a league in Milan to promote women's suffrage.

Writers of the time, including Giuseppe Acerbi, noted that Italian Romantics were merely mimicking the trends of foreign nations in a hasty way. In his view, their work lacked the depth of foreign writers.

Pietro Borsieri depicted Romanticism in Italy as a literary movement that was self-defined by the writers themselves. This fits the picture of isolated authors, with no single agreed meaning for the term.

Authors including Ludovico di Breme, Ermes Visconti and Giovanni Berchet classified themselves as Romantics, but others critiqued them. In her 1908 essay Il Romanticismo Italiano Non Esiste, Gina Martegiani wrote that they had only created two-dimensional imitations of German Romantic authors.

science.text: In 1906, the Italian Camillo Golgi and the Spaniard Santiago Ramón y Cajal were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on the structure of the nervous system. Ramón y Cajal was the first Spaniard to win a scientific Nobel Prize.
tags: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine

science.text: Alessandro Volta invented the voltaic pile in 1799 and reported it in a letter to the Royal Society in London, published in 1800. It showed that electricity could be generated chemically, overturning the theory that only living beings produced it. His work eventually led to the field of electrochemistry.

Isaac Peral designed the first electric-powered submarine, launched on September 8, 1888. In a test with naval authorities it made a simulated attack on a cruiser at night without being noticed, then returned to port undamaged.

Guglielmo Marconi is largely credited as the inventor of radio, thanks to his practical wireless telegraph system. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Ferdinand Braun. On 13 May 1897 he sent the first wireless communication over open sea, across the Bristol Channel.

In 1873 Camillo Golgi discovered a staining technique called the black reaction, a major breakthrough in neuroscience. Financial pressure had led him to become Chief Medical Officer in 1872 at the Hospital of the Chronically Ill (Pio Luogo degli Incurabili) at Abbiategrasso, near Milan. He set up a simple laboratory of his own in a refurbished kitchen of that hospital, and it was there that he made his most notable discoveries.

Santiago Ramón y Cajal's drawings of the tree-like growth of brain cells are still used for teaching. His artistic talents, which his father had not encouraged, contributed to his later success. He became director of the Instituto Nacional de Higiene in 1899.

In 1858 Stanislao Cannizzaro published a paper, Sunto di un corso di Filosofia chimica, insisting on the distinction between atomic and molecular weights that Amedeo Avogadro had earlier hypothesized. It showed how atomic weights could be deduced from the molecular weights of volatile compounds. The Royal Society awarded him its Copley Medal in 1891.

Amedeo Avogadro published an essay in 1811 containing his hypothesis, later known as Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. In 1911 a meeting in Turin marked the hundredth anniversary of the paper, attended by King Victor Emmanuel III.

Antonio Meucci set up a voice-communication link in his Staten Island home connecting his second-floor bedroom to his laboratory. He filed a patent caveat for his telephonic device in 1871, but in 1876 Alexander Graham Bell was granted the patent. In 2002 the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution acknowledging Meucci's work.

Isaac Peral destroyed the inside of his submarine and its plans to keep foreign spies from copying it, after a second project was rejected by naval authorities. He retired from the navy in November 1891 and founded an electric company in Madrid. There he patented an electric machine gun and drew blueprints for Spain's first electric power plants.

At Meucci's trial, his Memorandum Book of drawings and records from 1862 to 1882 was key evidence. The prosecutor accused him of backdating it, noting that the Rider & Clark company was founded only in 1863. Meucci said William E. Rider had given him a copy in 1862, but he was not believed.

Camillo Golgi was the first to dissect out intact nephrons in the kidney. He showed that the loop of Henle returns to the glomerulus it came from, a finding he published in 1889 after studying kidney function from 1882.

A detector preserved by the Science Museum Group, called the "Italian Navy" coherer, is linked to Marconi's December 1901 experiment. Studies say Marconi obtained it through Lieutenant Luigi Solari of the Royal Italian Navy. It is catalogued as a type of detector invented by Jagadish Chandra Bose in 1899, which sparked an attribution dispute.

politics.text: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, when Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia became King of Italy. It was created through the unification of several states in a decades-long process called the Risorgimento. The Savoy-led Kingdom of Sardinia was one of its legal predecessor states.

Before 1861, Italy was a peninsula of separate kingdoms, duchies and minor principalities, with many reigning dynasties. Southern Italy had not been united with northern Italy since the early medieval period, being mostly under the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

Napoleon was crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy at Milan Cathedral in 1805, restoring a Kingdom of Italy that lasted until 1814 with him as its only king. After his deposition, no Italian monarch claimed the overarching title until unification in 1861.

The architect of Italian unification was Count Camillo Benso di Cavour, Chief Minister of Victor Emmanuel. Rome itself remained under the Papacy for a further decade after 1861. In September 1870 invading Italian troops entered the Papal state, and the ensuing occupation made Rome part of the Kingdom of Italy. It forced Pope Pius IX into his palace, where he declared himself a prisoner in the Vatican, as did his successors until the Lateran Pacts of 1929.

The formerly republican leader Giuseppe Garibaldi made common cause with the House of Savoy to overthrow the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. The people then voted in a plebiscite to join Sardinia, forming the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

The Fasci Siciliani, a democratic and socialist movement that arose in Sicily between 1892 and 1893, was perceived as the "first act of Italian socialism". It was crushed after harsh military operations in 1894. Prime Minister Francesco Crispi pushed through exceptional laws against the Socialists from 1894, though they were ultimately unsuccessful.

In 1901, Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti tried to integrate the Socialist party, which had won 32 seats in the elections, into the government, but the party refused. From 1908 to 1912 there was cooperation with the bourgeois left, until radical syndicalism prevailed.

Italy took part in the Eight-Nation Alliance during the Boxer Rebellion in China from 1899 to 1901. The Qing Dynasty ceded a concession in Tientsin to Italy on 7 September 1901, and it was taken into Italian possession on 7 June 1902, run by an Italian consul.

philosophy.text: Italian idealism was born from interest in the German movement, especially Hegelian doctrine. It grew out of the spiritualism of the nineteenth-century Risorgimento tradition.

Scholastic thought began to flourish again, largely in reaction against Modernism inspired by Descartes, Kant and Hegel. Their principles were perceived to conflict with Christian dogma. This revival was particularly vigorous at first in Italy.

Antonio Rosmini (1797–1855) and Vincenzo Gioberti (1801–1852) both revived Augustinian neoplatonic themes, such as the interiority of conscience and divine illumination. Rosmini aspired to reform Kantianism in an ontological and transcendent sense.
Augusto Vera (1813–1885) wrote commentaries on Hegel and became a famous philosopher across Europe. He interpreted the Hegelian Absolute in a religious and transcendent sense.

Interest in Hegel spread in Italy especially through the works of Augusto Vera and Bertrando Spaventa (1817–1883). Francesco De Sanctis (1817–1883), author of the History of Italian Literature, also contributed studies on Hegelian "Aesthetic".

In the mid-19th century Italian Hegelians of the Risorgimento, active especially in Naples, included de Sanctis, Fiorentino and De Meis. They were contrasted by positivist thinkers such as Pasquale Villari.

Vincenzo Gioberti set out to counter the subjectivism of modern philosophy that came from Descartes. He reaffirmed the objective preeminence of God, or "Entity-Idea", and built on it an ontologism understood in an almost pantheistic manner.

After a parenthesis characterized by positivism, Giovanni Gentile published The reform of Hegelian dialectics in 1913. He resumed Spaventa's reading of the Hegelian Idea, seeing becoming in the Hegelian Spirit as coinciding with the pure act of thought.

The direct initiator of the neo-Scholastic movement in Italy was Gaetano Sanseverino (1811–1865), a canon at Naples. The German Jesuit Joseph Kleutgen, who taught at Rome, argued that post-Cartesian philosophy undermined Catholic theology.

Since 1913 Benedetto Croce opposed Gentile's vision. In his Essay on Hegel he read Hegelian thought as immanentist historicism and integrated the dialectic of opposites with that of the "distincts". Croce was the cousin of Bertrando Spaventa.

Kleutgen held that the remedy for post-Cartesian philosophy was the Aristotelian scientific method of Aquinas. From 1874 to 1891 the Accademia di San Tommaso of Rome published the review La Scienza Italiana. Its Italian writers stressed Scholastic metaphysics more than empirical sciences.

culture.text: Rome's tradition of high fashion dates back to 1871, when the city was proclaimed capital of the country. The Savoy court was established there, which brought new tailors and the birth of elegant ateliers.

In 1822, the antiquarian abbot Giovanni Battista Giani began excavating graves at Golasecca in Lombardy. He misidentified the clearly non-Roman burials as remains from the Battle of Ticinus of 218 BC between Hannibal and Scipio Africanus, and the culture later took its name from the site.

The first Italian film director is considered to be Vittorio Calcina, a collaborator of the Lumière brothers. In 1896 he filmed Pope Leo XIII, only a few months after the Lumière brothers began their motion picture exhibitions.

In 1865, the archaeologist Louis Laurent Gabriel de Mortillet correctly assigned the Golasecca tombs to a pre-Roman early Iron Age culture, likely with a Celtic substratum. He brought part of Abbot Giani's collection back to France for the Musée des Antiquités Nationales, where he was Vice-curator.

Pope Leo XIII, who reigned from 1878 to 1903, issued the encyclical Rerum novarum. It established modern Catholic social teaching and promoted labor rights, and a later pope chose the name Leo in reference to it.
The Italian film industry developed rapidly in the 1910s. In 1912, the year of greatest expansion, 569 films were produced in Turin, 420 in Rome and 120 in Milan.

The Golasecca culture's timeline became clearer in 1874, when French, Italian and German archaeologists met at the Archaeological Congress of Stockholm. Alexandre Bertrand, curator of the Musée des Antiquités Nationales, had excavated on site himself in 1873, and the culture was divided into three periods.
Cabiria, a 1914 epic directed by Giovanni Pastrone, is considered the most famous Italian silent film. It was also the first film in history to be shown in the White House.
